title: Labor Day is Basically New Year’s For Sports
subtitle: The unofficial end of summer also marks the busiest, most crowded stretch on the sports calendar.
contentHtml:
Hope you’re having a relaxing Labor Day! Enjoy this holiday-themed post, and we’ll be back in your inbox tomorrow with the usual programming.

Traditionally, Labor Day is the dividing line between summer and fall — culturally, at least, if not technically so (according to those annoying astronomical seasons).1 It has long marked the unofficial end of summer: the end of vacation and leisure season; the return of kids to school and adults to the regular grind of work; the start of Fall TV-season programming; and even the end of summer fashion conventions. (Famously, the rule is: “no white after Labor Day”.)

But the biggest dividing line of all for Labor Day — especially recently — might just be in the world of sports.

Subscribe now

The 2026 NFL season starts Wednesday (quick plug: check out my 📈2026 NFL Odds Tracker, Elo Ratings and Player Rankings🏈 page for a lot of goodies around the new season!), which leads into a Week 1 held immediately after Labor Day weekend. That’s no coincidence: ever since 2001, the league has deliberately placed the opening games of each season the weekend after Labor Day. From August 2000:

“People want to stretch those last, lazy days of summer.

That’s why the NFL has decided that this Sunday and Monday (September 3-4) will be the last time that it opens its season on Labor Day weekend.

Beginning with Labor Day, 2001, NFL fans will be able to enjoy the unofficial “end of summer” at the beach, in the country or at the barbecue, and then kick off fall with the opening of the NFL season on the weekend after Labor Day.”

In recent years, there have been calls for the NFL to “take back” Labor Day weekend as the league considers expanding to an 18-game regular season schedule. But for now, the convention is clear: Wear white all you want, but no pro football before Labor Day.

That’s just one aspect of the broader shift in the sports calendar around early September. While college football technically tends to place “Week Zero” at the tail-end of August, America’s second-favorite sport only truly rolls into action when the calendar flips to the ninth month. The same goes for Europe’s favorite sport as well — club-soccer leagues like the Premier League begin in mid-August when there isn’t a World Cup, and late August when (like this year) there is. But only now, in September, has the season gotten in full swing.

That’s in addition to the sports that are already in action, and have been for a while, such as baseball, tennis, golf, WNBA, NASCAR, F1 and U.S. club soccer leagues like the MLS and NWSL. Borrowing from a chart I first made for this NASCAR story, here’s a visualization of each major sport/event in action each month, based on the rough share of the month it was active:

If you simply add up all the sport values running concurrently each month, only October — with a total value of 10.71 out of a possible 15 sports — rates higher than September (at 9.90), which in turn checks in ahead of November (9.50), March (9.29), May (9.29) and April (9.23).

What makes September truly the most important pivot point on the schedule, though, is not just its volume, but also the velocity of change in the sporting calendar that it brings. No month features more of a positive change in total active sports versus the month before than, you guessed it, September:

The biggest ramp-up months on the U.S. sports calendar

September is also unique in that none of the sports active within it are decreasing in activity — they’re only increasing (or staying level). No other month — not even mighty October, which sees the WNBA ramp down — can say that.

And of course, September also sets into motion the unparalleled three-month corridor of sports activity that is September/October/November, with the NBA, NHL and college hoops joining the party as well.

All of which is to say, as sports fans, “Happy New Year”! Labor Day not only represents the end of Summer, it also means the changing of the sports calendar into something more active and also simply different than what came before. So welcome to the busiest stretch of the sports year — and I hope you cleared your real-life calendar.

I’ve always favored defining the seasons along meteorological lines instead — Fall is September/October/November, Winter is December/January/February, Spring is March/April/May and Summer is June/July/August. Screw your solstices and equinoxes!
